problems.problem: A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ is such that the polynomial $(f(x))^3 - f(x)$ has exactly three real roots. Find the ordinate of the vertex of the graph of this trinomial.
Prove that there exists a positive integer $n > 1$ such that the product of some $n$ consecutive positive integers is equal to the product of some $n + 100$ consecutive positive integers.

Kostya had two sets of 17 coins each: in one set all coins are genuine, and in the other exactly 5 are counterfeit (all coins look the same; all genuine coins weigh the same, all counterfeit coins also weigh the same, but it is unknown whether they are lighter or heavier than the genuine ones). Kostya gave one of the sets to a friend and later forgot which of the two sets he had kept. Can Kostya find out, using two weighings on a balance scale without weights, which of the two sets he gave away?

Circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ touch externally at a point $O$. Points $A$ and $B$ on the circle $\omega_1$ and points $C$ and $D$ on the circle $\omega_2$ are such that $AC$ and $BD$ are the common external tangents of the circles. The line $AO$ meets the segment $CD$ at a point $M$, and the line $CO$ meets the circle $\omega_1$ for the second time at a point $N$. Prove that the points $B$, $M$ and $N$ are collinear.
A positive integer $m$ is such that the sum of the digits in the decimal representation of the number $2^m$ is equal to 8. Can the last digit of the number $2^m$ be equal to 6?

The circle $\omega$ inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively. On the extension of the segment $AA_1$ beyond the point $A$ a point $D$ is taken such that $AD = AC_1$. The lines $DB_1$ and $DC_1$ meet the circle $\omega$ for the second time at the points $B_2$ and $C_2$. Prove that $B_2C_2$ is a diameter of the circle $\omega$.

Positive numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{2009}$ satisfy the equalities
$$x_1^2 - x_1x_2 + x_2^2 = x_2^2 - x_2x_3 + x_3^2 = x_3^2 - x_3x_4 + x_4^2 = \ldots = x_{2008}^2 - x_{2008}x_{2009} + x_{2009}^2 = x_{2009}^2 - x_{2009}x_1 + x_1^2.$$
Prove that the numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{2009}$ are equal.

At a party, a company of 20 people has to be seated at 4 tables. A seating is called successful if any two people sitting at the same table are friends. It turned out that successful seatings exist, and in every successful seating exactly 5 people sit at each table. What is the largest possible number of pairs of friends in this company?

Nine skiers left the start one after another and covered the course, each at his own constant speed. Could it happen that each skier took part in exactly four overtakings? (Exactly two skiers take part in each overtaking: the one who overtakes and the one who is overtaken.)

Is it possible, for some positive integer $k$, to split all the positive integers from 1 to $k$ into two groups and write the numbers of each group one after another in some order so that two equal numbers are obtained?

In a triangle $ABC$ the angle bisectors $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ are drawn, meeting at the point $I$. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $AD$ meets the lines $BE$ and $CF$ at the points $M$ and $N$, respectively. Prove that the points $A$, $I$, $M$ and $N$ lie on a circle.

Call a positive integer $b$ lucky if for every positive integer $a$ such that $a^5$ is divisible by $b^2$, the number $a^2$ is divisible by $b$. Find the number of lucky positive integers less than 2010.
Nonzero numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $ax^2 + bx + c > cx$ for every $x$. Prove that $cx^2 - bx + a > cx - b$ for every $x$.

The lines touching a circle $\omega$ at the points $B$ and $D$ meet at a point $P$. A line through $P$ cuts a chord $AC$ out of the circle. Through an arbitrary point of the segment $AC$ a line parallel to $BD$ is drawn. Prove that it divides the lengths of the broken lines $ABC$ and $ADC$ in the same ratio.
Do there exist three pairwise distinct nonzero integers whose sum is zero and the sum of whose thirteenth powers is the square of some positive integer?

A staircase of height $n$ is the figure consisting of all cells of an $n \times n$ square lying not above the diagonal (the figure shows a staircase of height 4). In how many different ways can a staircase of height $n$ be divided into several rectangles whose sides go along the grid lines and whose areas are pairwise distinct?

Two runners started simultaneously from the same point. First they ran along a street to the stadium, and then to the finish, three laps around the stadium. Both ran the whole distance at constant speeds, and during the race the first runner overtook the second one twice. Prove that the first ran at least twice as fast as the second.

Points $M$ and $K$ are chosen on the side $AC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ so that $\angle ABM = \angle CBK$. Prove that the centres of the circles circumscribed about the triangles $ABM$, $ABK$, $CBM$ and $CBK$ lie on a circle.

Distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{14}$ are given. All 196 numbers of the form $a_k + a_\ell$, where $1 \leqslant k, \ell \leqslant 14$, are written on the board. Can it happen that for every combination of two digits there is at least one number on the board ending in this combination (that is, there are numbers ending in $00, 01, 02, \ldots, 99$)?

Nonzero numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that any two of the three equations $ax^{11} + bx^4 + c = 0$, $bx^{11} + cx^4 + a = 0$, $cx^{11} + ax^4 + b = 0$ have a common root. Prove that all three equations have a common root.
Find all numbers $a$ such that for every positive integer $n$ the number $an(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)$ is an integer.
2011 numbers are written on the board. It turned out that the sum of any three of the written numbers is also a written number. What is the smallest possible number of zeros among these numbers?

In a scalene acute triangle $ABC$ the points $C_0$ and $B_0$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, $O$ is the circumcentre and $H$ is the orthocentre. The lines $BH$ and $OC_0$ meet at a point $P$, and the lines $CH$ and $OB_0$ meet at a point $Q$. It turned out that the quadrilateral $OPHQ$ is a rhombus. Prove that the points $A$, $P$ and $Q$ are collinear.

A straight stick 2 metres long was sawn into $N$ sticks, the length of each of which is an integer number of centimetres. For what smallest $N$ can one guarantee that, using all the resulting sticks and without breaking them, one can form the outline of some rectangle?

Ten positive numbers are given, any two of which are distinct. Prove that among them there are either three numbers whose product is greater than the product of some two of the remaining ones, or three numbers whose product is greater than the product of some four of the remaining ones.
A convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ is given. It is known that $\angle FAE = \angle BDC$ and that the quadrilaterals $ABDF$ and $ACDE$ are cyclic. Prove that the lines $BF$ and $CE$ are parallel.

A sequence of numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ is defined by the conditions $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 143$ and
$$a_{n+1} = 5 \cdot \frac{a_1 + a_2 + \ldots + a_n}{n}$$
for all $n \geqslant 2$. Prove that all terms of the sequence are integers.

$2N$ points are marked on a circle ($N$ is a positive integer). It is known that through any point inside the circle there pass at most two chords with endpoints at the marked points. A matching is a set of $N$ chords with endpoints at the marked points such that each marked point is an endpoint of exactly one of these chords. A matching is called even if the number of points at which its chords intersect is even, and odd otherwise. Find the difference between the number of even and the number of odd matchings.

A convex pentagon is given. Petya wrote down in his notebook the values of the sines of all its angles, and Vasya the values of the cosines of all its angles. It turned out that among the numbers written by Petya there are no four distinct ones. Can all the numbers written by Vasya be distinct?

Petya chose a positive integer $a > 1$ and wrote fifteen numbers $1 + a, 1 + a^2, 1 + a^3, \ldots, 1 + a^{15}$ on the board. Then he erased several numbers so that any two of the remaining numbers are coprime. What is the largest possible number of numbers that could remain on the board?

An $n \times n$ square is given. Initially its cells are coloured white and black in a chessboard pattern, and at least one of the corner cells is black. In one move it is allowed to recolour simultaneously the four cells of some $2 \times 2$ square according to the following rule: each white cell is recoloured black, each black cell green, and each green cell white. For which $n$ can one obtain, after several moves, a chessboard colouring in which black and white have swapped places?

In a trapezoid $ABCD$ the lateral side $CD$ is perpendicular to the bases, and $O$ is the intersection point of the diagonals. On the circumcircle of the triangle $OCD$ a point $S$ diametrically opposite to the point $O$ is taken. Prove that $\angle BSC = \angle ASD$.

Positive integers $M$ and $N$, both greater than ten, have the same number of digits and satisfy $M = 3N$. To obtain the number $M$, one has to add 2 to one of the digits of $N$ and add an odd digit to each of the remaining digits. What digit could the number $N$ end with? Find all possible answers.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn. The circle $\Omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ meets the line $A_1C_1$ at the points $A'$ and $C'$. The tangents to $\Omega$ at the points $A'$ and $C'$ meet at a point $B'$. Prove that the line $BB'$ passes through the centre of the circle $\Omega$.

Three quadratic trinomials $P(x)$, $Q(x)$ and $R(x)$ with positive leading coefficients are given, each having two distinct roots. It turned out that substituting the roots of the trinomial $R(x)$ into the polynomial $P(x) + Q(x)$ gives equal values. Similarly, substituting the roots of the trinomial $P(x)$ into the polynomial $Q(x) + R(x)$ gives equal values, and substituting the roots of the trinomial $Q(x)$ into the polynomial $P(x) + R(x)$ gives equal values. Prove that the three numbers, the sum of the roots of $P(x)$, the sum of the roots of $Q(x)$ and the sum of the roots of $R(x)$, are equal to each other.

Can the set of all positive integers be partitioned into pairwise disjoint finite subsets $A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots$ so that for every positive integer $k$ the sum of all the numbers in the subset $A_k$ equals $k + 2013$?

Thirty girls, 13 in red dresses and 17 in blue dresses, danced in a ring around a New Year tree. Afterwards each of them was asked whether her neighbour on the right was in a blue dress. It turned out that exactly those girls answered correctly who stood between two girls in dresses of the same colour. How many girls could have answered in the affirmative?
Positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$, where $c \geqslant 2$, are such that $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = \frac{1}{c}$. Prove that at least one of the numbers $a + c$, $b + c$ is composite.

Three common tangents are drawn to two non-intersecting circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$: two external ones, $a$ and $b$, and one internal one, $c$. The lines $a$, $b$ and $c$ touch the circle $\omega_1$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively, and the circle $\omega_2$ at the points $A_2$, $B_2$ and $C_2$, respectively. Prove that the ratio of the areas of the triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $A_2B_2C_2$ is equal to the ratio of the radii of the circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.

2013 points dividing a circle of length 2013 into equal arcs are marked on it. There is a counter at each marked point. The distance between two points is the length of the smaller arc between them. For what largest $n$ can the counters be rearranged so that again there is a counter at each marked point, and the distance between any two counters that were initially at distance at most $n$ from each other has increased?
In one week a pupil received 17 marks (each of them is 2, 3, 4 or 5). The arithmetic mean of these 17 marks is an integer. Prove that he received some mark at most twice.

Call a hundred-digit number $n$ unusual if the decimal representation of $n^3$ ends in $n$ while the decimal representation of $n^2$ does not end in $n$. Prove that there exist at least two hundred-digit unusual numbers.

The language of the AU tribe has two letters, "a" and "u". Some sequences of these letters are words, and each word has at most 13 letters. It is known that if any two words are written one after the other, the resulting sequence of letters is not a word. Find the largest possible number of words in such a language.

Points $C_1$ and $C_2$ are chosen on the side $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$. Similarly, points $A_1$ and $A_2$ are chosen on the side $BC$, and points $B_1$ and $B_2$ on the side $AC$. It turned out that the segments $A_1B_2$, $B_1C_2$ and $C_1A_2$ have equal lengths, meet at one point, and the angle between any two of them is $60^\circ$. Prove that
$$\frac{A_1A_2}{BC} = \frac{B_1B_2}{CA} = \frac{C_1C_2}{AB}.$$

The equation $x^3 + {*}x^2 + {*}x + {*} = 0$ is written on the board. Petya and Vasya in turn replace the asterisks by rational numbers: first Petya replaces any of the asterisks, then Vasya any of the two remaining ones, and then Petya the remaining asterisk. Is it true that, whatever Vasya does, Petya can obtain an equation two of whose roots differ by 2014?

A triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$ with centre $O$. The circle constructed on $AO$ as a diameter meets the circumcircle of the triangle $OBC$ at a point $S \neq O$. The tangents to $\Omega$ at the points $B$ and $C$ meet at a point $P$. Prove that the points $A$, $S$ and $P$ are collinear.

$10^{1000}$ positive integers stand around a circle. Between every two neighbouring numbers their least common multiple was written. Can these least common multiples form $10^{1000}$ consecutive numbers (arranged in some order)?

Petya placed several counters on a $50 \times 50$ board, at most one in each cell. Prove that Vasya can place at most 99 new counters (possibly none) on free cells of the same board so that there is still at most one counter in each cell, and every row and every column of the board contains an even number of counters.

Integers $a, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{13}$ are such that
$$a = (1+x_1)(1+x_2)\ldots(1+x_{13}) = (1-x_1)(1-x_2)\ldots(1-x_{13}).$$
Prove that $ax_1x_2\ldots x_{13} = 0$.

All the vertices of a regular $n$-gon and also its centre were marked in the plane. Then the outline of this $n$-gon was drawn and the centre was joined with all the vertices; as a result the $n$-gon was divided into $n$ triangles. Vasya wrote a number at each marked point (some of the numbers may be equal). Into each triangle of the division he wrote, in arbitrary order, the three numbers standing at its vertices; after that he erased the numbers at the marked points. For which $n$ can Petya always restore the number at each marked point from the triples of numbers written in the triangles?

Let $AL$ be an angle bisector of a triangle $ABC$. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $AL$ meets the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ at the points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that the circle circumscribed about the triangle $PLQ$ touches the side $BC$.

Positive numbers $a, b, c$ satisfy $ab + bc + ca = 1$. Prove that
$$\sqrt{a + \frac{1}{a}} + \sqrt{b + \frac{1}{b}} + \sqrt{c + \frac{1}{c}} \geqslant 2(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c}).$$

After watching a film, viewers rated it one after another with an integer number of points from 0 to 10. At every moment the rating of the film was computed as the sum of all marks given divided by their number. At some moment $T$ the rating turned out to be an integer, and after that it decreased by one with each new voting viewer. What is the largest possible number of viewers who could have voted after the moment $T$?

A right triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$ is given. Let $BK$ be an angle bisector of this triangle. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $AKB$ meets the side $BC$ for the second time at a point $L$. Prove that $CB + CL = AB$.

The coefficients $a$, $b$, $c$ of a quadratic trinomial $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ are positive integers whose sum is 2000. Pasha may change any coefficient by 1, paying 1 rouble. Prove that he can obtain a quadratic trinomial having at least one integer root by paying at most 1050 roubles.

A positive integer $n \geqslant 2$ is given. Consider all colourings of the cells of an $n \times n$ board in $k$ colours such that each cell is painted in exactly one colour and all $k$ colours occur. For what smallest $k$ does every such colouring contain four cells painted in four different colours located at the intersection of two rows and two columns?

Quadratic trinomials $f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_{100}(x)$ are given with equal coefficients of $x^2$, equal coefficients of $x$, but distinct constant terms; each of them has two roots. For each trinomial $f_i(x)$ one root was chosen and denoted by $x_i$. What values can the sum $f_2(x_1) + f_3(x_2) + \ldots + f_{100}(x_{99}) + f_1(x_{100})$ take?

Petya chose 10 consecutive positive integers and wrote each of them either with a red or with a blue pencil (both colours are present). Can the sum of the least common multiple of all the red numbers and the least common multiple of all the blue numbers end in 2016?

Points $K$ and $L$ are taken on the side $AB$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ (the point $K$ lies between $A$ and $L$), and points $M$ and $N$ on the side $CD$ (the point $M$ lies between $C$ and $N$). It is known that $AK = KN = DN$ and $BL = BC = CM$. Prove that if $BCNK$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, then $ADML$ is cyclic too.

The cells of a $100 \times 100$ grid table are painted black and white. All columns contain equally many black cells, while all rows contain different numbers of black cells. What is the largest possible number of pairs of differently coloured cells sharing a side?

Call a nonempty (finite or infinite) set $A$ of real numbers complete if for any real numbers $a$ and $b$ (not necessarily distinct and not necessarily lying in $A$) such that $a + b$ lies in $A$, the number $ab$ also lies in $A$. Find all complete sets of real numbers.

Inside an isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $BC$ and $AD$ there is a circle $\omega$ with centre $I$ touching the segments $AB$, $CD$ and $DA$. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $BIC$ meets the side $AB$ for the second time at a point $E$. Prove that the line $CE$ touches the circle $\omega$.

$n$ boys and $n$ girls stand around a circle. Call a pair consisting of a boy and a girl good if on one of the arcs between them there are equally many boys and girls (in particular, a boy and a girl standing next to each other form a good pair). It turned out that there is a girl who belongs to exactly 10 good pairs. Prove that there is also a boy who belongs to exactly 10 good pairs.
Find all pairs of distinct real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $x^{100} - y^{100} = 2^{99}(x - y)$ and $x^{200} - y^{200} = 2^{199}(x - y)$.
In a product of five positive integers, each factor was decreased by 3. Could the product have increased exactly 15 times as a result?

A circle with centre $I$ is inscribed in a quadrilateral $ABCD$. The rays $BA$ and $CD$ meet at a point $P$, and the rays $AD$ and $BC$ meet at a point $Q$. It is known that the point $P$ lies on the circle $\omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $AIC$. Prove that the point $Q$ also lies on the circle $\omega$.

Pasha chose 2017 (not necessarily distinct) positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2017}$ and plays the following game with himself. Initially he has an unlimited supply of stones and 2017 large empty boxes. In one move Pasha adds $a_1$ stones to any box (of his choice), $a_2$ stones to any of the remaining boxes (of his choice), $\ldots$, and finally $a_{2017}$ stones to the remaining box. Pasha's goal is to achieve that after some move all boxes contain equally many stones. Could he have chosen the numbers so that the goal can be achieved in 43 moves but not in any smaller nonzero number of moves?

A teacher is going to give the children a problem of the following kind. He will tell them that he has chosen a polynomial $P(x)$ of degree 2017 with integer coefficients whose leading coefficient equals 1. Then he will tell them $k$ integers $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$, and separately the value of the expression $P(n_1) \cdot P(n_2) \cdot \ldots \cdot P(n_k)$. From these data the children must find a polynomial that the teacher could have chosen. For what smallest $k$ can the teacher compose a problem of this kind so that the polynomial found by the children necessarily coincides with the chosen one?

Oleg drew an empty $50 \times 50$ table and wrote a nonzero number above each column and to the left of each row. It turned out that all 100 written numbers are distinct, and 50 of them are rational while the remaining 50 are irrational. Then in each cell of the table he wrote the product of the numbers written next to its row and its column (a "multiplication table"). What is the largest number of products in this table that could be rational?

Initially several (more than one) positive integers are written on the board. Then every minute a number equal to the sum of the squares of all numbers already written on the board is added to it (thus, if the numbers 1, 2, 2 were initially written on the board, then in the first minute the number $1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2$ would be added). Prove that the hundredth added number has at least 100 distinct prime divisors.
A convex polygon is cut by non-intersecting diagonals into isosceles triangles. Prove that this polygon has two equal sides.

A circle $\omega$ is circumscribed about an acute triangle $ABC$. A point $D$ is chosen on the side $AB$ and a point $E$ on the side $BC$ so that $AC \parallel DE$. Points $P$ and $Q$ on the smaller arc $AC$ of the circle $\omega$ are such that $DP \parallel EQ$. The rays $QA$ and $PC$ meet the line $DE$ at the points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that $\angle XBY + \angle PBQ = 180^\circ$.
Divide some grid square into grid squares so that not all the small squares are equal, but there is the same number of small squares of each size.

Petya and Vasya take turns writing on the board positive integers not exceeding 2018 (writing a number already present is forbidden); Petya starts. If after a player's move there are three numbers on the board forming an arithmetic progression, this player wins. Which of the players has a strategy guaranteeing a win?
Positive numbers $x$, $y$ are such that $x^5 - y^3 \geqslant 2x$. Prove that $x^3 \geqslant 2y$.

Let $O$ be the centre of the circle $\Omega$ circumscribed about an acute triangle $ABC$. A point $P$ is taken on the arc $AC$ of this circle not containing the point $B$. A point $X$ is chosen on the segment $BC$ so that $PX \perp AC$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $BXP$ lies on the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABO$.

An odd number $n > 10$ is given. Find the number of ways to arrange the positive integers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$ around a circle in some order so that each number is a divisor of the sum of its two neighbours. (Arrangements differing by a rotation or a reflection are considered the same.)

Petya chose a positive integer $n$ and wrote the following $n$ fractions on the board:
$$\frac{0}{n}, \frac{1}{n-1}, \frac{2}{n-2}, \frac{3}{n-3}, \ldots, \frac{n-1}{n-(n-1)}.$$
Let the number $n$ be divisible by a positive integer $d$. Prove that among the written fractions there is a fraction equal to the number $d - 1$.
A convex quadrilateral is assembled from four equal triangles. Is it true that this quadrilateral necessarily has parallel sides?

A $1000 \times 1000$ grid board is given. A piece called a cheetah standing on an arbitrary cell $x$ attacks all cells of the $19 \times 19$ square with central cell $x$, except the cells lying in the same column or the same row as $x$. What is the largest number of cheetahs not attacking each other that can be placed on the board?
Prove that there exists a positive integer $n > 10^{2018}$ such that the sum of all primes less than $n$ is coprime to $n$.

A triangle $ABC$ with $\angle A = \angle C = 30^\circ$ is given. Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are chosen on its sides $AB$, $BC$ and $AC$, respectively, so that $\angle BFD = \angle BFE = 60^\circ$. The perimeter of the triangle $ABC$ is $p$, and the perimeter of the triangle $DEF$ is $p_1$. Prove that $p \leqslant 2p_1$.

Each of 10 people is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Each of them thought of some number (not necessarily an integer). Then the first said: "My number is greater than 1", the second said: "My number is greater than 2", $\ldots$, the tenth said: "My number is greater than 10". After that all ten, speaking in some order, said: "My number is less than 1", "My number is less than 2", $\ldots$, "My number is less than 10" (each said exactly one of these ten phrases). What is the largest possible number of knights among these 10 people?

A convex quadrilateral of perimeter $10^{100}$ is given, all of whose side lengths are positive integers, and the sum of the lengths of any three sides is divisible by the length of the remaining fourth side. Prove that this quadrilateral is a rhombus.

The cells of a $2 \times 2019$ table have to be filled with numbers (exactly one number in each cell) according to the following rules. The top row must contain 2019 real numbers, no two of which are equal, and the bottom row must contain the same 2019 numbers but in a different order. Each of the 2019 columns must contain two different numbers whose sum is a rational number. What is the largest possible number of irrational numbers in the first row of the table?

An infinite sequence of nonzero numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ is such that for all positive integers $n \geqslant 2018$ the number $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest root of the polynomial
$$P_n(x) = x^{2n} + a_1x^{2n-2} + a_2x^{2n-4} + \ldots + a_n.$$
Prove that there exists $N$ such that in the infinite sequence $a_N, a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \ldots$ each term is less than the previous one.

In a scalene triangle $ABC$ the angle bisector $BL$ is drawn. The extension of the median drawn from the vertex $B$ meets the circle $\omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ at a point $D$. Through the circumcentre of the triangle $BDL$ a line $\ell$ parallel to the line $AC$ is drawn. Prove that the circle $\omega$ touches the line $\ell$.
Four consecutive positive integers greater than 100 are given. Prove that one can choose three of them whose sum can be represented as the product of three distinct positive integers greater than 1.

Real numbers $a$ and $b$ with $b > a > 1$ are given. Let
$$x_n = 2^n\left(\sqrt[2^n]{b} - \sqrt[2^n]{a}\right).$$
Prove that the sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ is decreasing.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitude $BH$ is drawn. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the segments $AH$ and $CH$, respectively. In the circle $\Omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $BMN$ the diameter $BB'$ is drawn. Prove that $AB' = CB'$.

A convex $n$-gon ($n \geqslant 4$) is drawn on the board. Each of its vertices has to be painted either black or white. Call a diagonal multicoloured if its endpoints have different colours. Call a colouring of the vertices good if the $n$-gon can be divided into triangles by multicoloured diagonals having no common points (except vertices). Find the number of good colourings.

A sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ is defined by the conditions $a_1 = 1$, $a_{n+1} = a_n + a_{[\sqrt{n}]}$ for all positive integers $n \geqslant 1$. Prove that for every positive integer $k$ this sequence contains a term divisible by $k$. (As usual, $[x]$ denotes the largest integer not exceeding $x$.)
Find at least one four-digit number with the following property: if the sum of all digits of this number is multiplied by the product of all its digits, the result is 3990.

A set $A$ consists of $n$ distinct positive integers whose sum equals $n^2$. A set $B$ also consists of $n$ distinct positive integers whose sum equals $n^2$. Prove that there is a number belonging both to the set $A$ and to the set $B$.

Kolya and Dima play a game on an $8 \times 8$ board, moving alternately; Kolya starts. Kolya draws crosses in cells, and Dima covers pairs of side-adjacent cells of the board with $1 \times 2$ rectangles (dominoes). On his move Kolya must put one cross into any empty cell (i.e. a cell in which no cross has been drawn yet and which is not yet covered by a domino). On his move Dima must cover with a domino two cells (not yet covered by other dominoes) containing an even total number of crosses (0 or 2). The player who cannot make a move loses. Which of the players has a winning strategy?

Let $p$ be a prime greater than 3. Prove that there exists a positive integer $y$ less than $p/2$ such that the number $py + 1$ cannot be represented as a product of two integers each greater than $y$.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is circumscribed about a circle $\omega$. Prove that the diameter of the circle $\omega$ does not exceed the length of the segment joining the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AD$.

The expression $\cos x$ is written on the board. It is allowed to add or multiply several expressions written on the board (one expression may be used several times) and to write the new expression obtained on the board. Is it possible, after several operations, to obtain an expression that takes the value 0 at $x = \pi$?

Rectangles are constructed outwards on the sides of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. It turned out that all vertices of these rectangles other than the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on one circle. Prove that the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic.

$n$ quadratic trinomials of the form ${*}x^2 + {*}x + {*}$ are written on the board (asterisks are written instead of the coefficients). Is it possible, for some $n > 100$, to put in place of the $3n$ asterisks some $3n$ consecutive positive integers (in some order) so that each of the $n$ trinomials has two distinct integer roots?

Call a polygon good if it has a pair of parallel sides. A regular polygon was cut by diagonals not intersecting (at interior points) into several polygons so that all these polygons have the same odd number of sides. Can it happen that at least one of these polygons is good?

Petya has thought of two polynomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, each of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$ (i.e. the degree of each polynomial does not exceed 2). In one move Vasya tells Petya a number $t$, and Petya tells him (at his own discretion) one of the values $f(t)$ or $g(t)$ (without specifying which one he reported). After $n$ moves Vasya must determine one of Petya's polynomials. For what smallest $n$ does Vasya have a strategy that guarantees this?

A first-grader made two triangles out of six sticks. Then he took the triangles apart and split the six sticks into two groups of three: the first group consisted of the three longest sticks and the second of the three shortest. Is it necessarily possible to make a triangle out of the three sticks of the first group? And out of the three sticks of the second group?
Two nonzero numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the inequalities $x^4 - y^4 > x$ and $y^4 - x^4 > y$. Can the product $xy$ be a negative number?

Let $S$ be a set of positive integers. It turned out that for every number $a$ of the set $S$ there exist two numbers $b$ and $c$ of the set $S$ such that
$$a = \frac{b(3c - 5)}{15}.$$
Prove that the set $S$ is infinite.

The incircle touches the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ of a scalene triangle $ABC$ at the points $C_1$, $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively. Let $m$ be the midline of the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ parallel to the side $B_1C_1$. The bisector of the angle $B_1A_1C_1$ meets $m$ at a point $K$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $BCK$ touches $m$.

Petya and Vasya play on a $100 \times 100$ board. Initially all cells of the board are white. With each of his moves Petya paints black one or several white cells standing consecutively along a diagonal. With each of his moves Vasya paints black one or several white cells standing consecutively along a vertical. (The figure shows possible first moves of Petya and Vasya on a $4 \times 4$ board.) Petya makes the first move. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who wins with correct play?

Three positive integers were written on the board: two ten-digit numbers $a$ and $b$, and also their sum $a + b$. What is the largest possible number of odd digits written on the board?

Vasya wrote the positive integers from 1 to 81 in the cells of a $9 \times 9$ table (one number in each cell, all numbers distinct). It turned out that any two numbers differing by 3 stand in cells sharing a side. Is it true that there must be two corner cells the difference of whose numbers is divisible by 6?

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the base $AC$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$. On the extensions of the segments $AC$ and $BC$ beyond the point $C$ the points $D$ and $K$, respectively, are marked so that $BC = CD$ and $CM = CK$. Prove that the circles circumscribed about the triangles $ABD$ and $MCK$ touch each other.

A magician and his assistant are going to show the following trick. They have $n \geqslant 3$ cards with the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$, and a row of $n$ card-sized cells. The backs of all cards are indistinguishable. A spectator puts the cards 1 and 2 on some two places; the magician's assistant, seeing this, puts the remaining cards on the free places. Then all cards are turned face down, and the magician enters. He turns over one of the cards, and then the spectator turns over another one. After that the magician must correctly point out card 1 and correctly point out card 2. For which $n$ can the magician and the assistant agree so that the trick is guaranteed to succeed?

Vitya wrote $n$ distinct positive integers in a notebook. For each pair of numbers from the notebook he wrote their least common multiple on the board. Could it happen, for some $n > 100$, that the $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ numbers on the board are (in some order) consecutive terms of a non-constant arithmetic progression?

One day after classes Misha wrote ten positive integers on a sheet of paper. All ten numbers are pairwise distinct. It is known that three numbers divisible by 5 can be chosen from the ten written numbers. It is also known that four numbers divisible by 4 can be chosen from the ten written numbers. Can the sum of all the written numbers be less than 75?

A quadratic trinomial $P(x)$ is given. Prove that there exist pairwise distinct numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that the equalities
$$P(b+c) = P(a), \quad P(c+a) = P(b), \quad P(a+b) = P(c)$$
hold.

Vasya has $n$ sweets of several kinds, where $n \geqslant 145$. It is known that if any group containing at least 145 sweets is chosen from these $n$ sweets (in particular, the group of all $n$ sweets may be chosen), then there is a kind of sweets such that the chosen group contains exactly 10 sweets of this kind. Find the largest possible value of $n$.

Let $P(x) = a_nx^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \ldots + a_1x + a_0$, where $n$ is a positive integer. It is known that the numbers $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are integers, $a_n \neq 0$, $a_{n-k} = a_k$ for all $k = 0, 1, \ldots, n$, and $a_n + a_{n-1} + \ldots + a_1 + a_0 = 0$. Prove that the number $P(2022)$ is divisible by the square of some positive integer greater than 1.

A hexagon $AECDBF$ is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$. It is known that the point $D$ bisects the arc $BC$, and that the triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ have a common incircle. The line $BC$ meets the segments $DF$ and $DE$ at the points $X$ and $Y$, and the line $EF$ meets the segments $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $Z$ and $T$, respectively. Prove that the points $X$, $Y$, $T$, $Z$ lie on a circle.
Three consecutive odd numbers are written on the board. Can the sum of the remainders of these three numbers upon division by 2022 be a prime number?
A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $\angle A = 2\angle B$ is given. The bisector of the angle $C$ meets the side $AB$ at a point $E$. Prove that $AD + AE = BE$.
$N$ points are marked in the plane. Any three of them form a triangle whose angles, measured in degrees, are positive integers. For what largest $N$ is this possible?

At the vertices of a regular 100-gon, 100 counters are placed, bearing the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 100$ in exactly this order clockwise. In one move it is allowed to swap two counters standing at neighbouring vertices, provided that the numbers of these counters differ by at most $k$. For what smallest $k$ can one achieve, by a series of such moves, an arrangement in which every counter is shifted by one position clockwise (relative to its initial position)?
Prove that there exists a positive integer $b$ such that for every positive integer $n > b$ the sum of the digits of the number $n!$ is at least $10^{100}$.

Zeros are initially written in a $6 \times 6$ table. In one operation one may choose a cell and replace the number in it by any integer. Is it possible, in 8 operations, to obtain a table in which all 12 sums of the numbers in the rows and columns are distinct positive numbers?

A paper triangle with side lengths 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm is given. Can it be cut into several (more than one) polygons each of which has area (measured in cm$^2$) numerically equal to its perimeter (measured in cm)?

In the city N, 50 city olympiads in different subjects took place; exactly 30 schoolchildren took part in each of these olympiads, but no two olympiads had the same set of participants. It is known that for any 30 olympiads there is a schoolchild who took part in all these 30 olympiads. Prove that there is a schoolchild who took part in all 50 olympiads.
Positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ are given such that $a > 1$, $b > c > 1$, and the number $abc + 1$ is divisible by $ab - b + 1$. Prove that $b$ is divisible by $a$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitude $BD$ is drawn and the orthocentre $H$ is marked. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $HD$ meets the circle circumscribed about the triangle $BCD$ at the points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $\angle APB + \angle AQB = 180^\circ$.
For a positive integer $n$ denote by $S_n$ the least common multiple of all the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$. Does there exist a positive integer $m$ such that $S_{m+1} = 4S_m$?

Petya took some three-digit positive integers $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_9$ and wrote on the board the equation
$$a_9x^9 + a_8x^8 + \ldots + a_2x^2 + a_1x + a_0 = *.$$
Prove that Vasya can write in place of the asterisk some 30-digit positive integer so that the resulting equation has an integer root.

The bisector of the angle $A$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meets the side $BC$ at a point $K$. A point $L$ is chosen on the side $AB$ so that $AL = CK$. The segments $AK$ and $CL$ meet at a point $M$. On the extension of the segment $AD$ beyond the point $D$ a point $N$ is marked. It is known that the quadrilateral $ALMN$ is cyclic. Prove that $\angle CNL = 90^\circ$.

A positive integer $k$ is given. $n$ poles stand at equal intervals along a road. Misha painted them in $k$ colours and, for each pair of poles of the same colour with no other pole of that colour between them, computed the distance between them. All these distances turned out to be distinct. For what largest $n$ could this happen?

Prove that for any three positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ the inequality
$$(x - y)\sqrt{3x^2 + y^2} + (y - z)\sqrt{3y^2 + z^2} + (z - x)\sqrt{3z^2 + x^2} \geqslant 0$$
holds.

Oleg has a set of 2024 distinct grid rectangles of sizes $1 \times 1$, $1 \times 2$, $1 \times 3$, $\ldots$, $1 \times 2024$ (one rectangle of each size). Can he, choosing some of them, assemble a grid square of area greater than 1?

The parabola $y = x^2$ is drawn in the coordinate plane. For a given number $k > 0$ consider the trapezoids inscribed in this parabola (that is, all vertices of the trapezoid lie on the parabola) whose bases are parallel to the $x$-axis and the product of the lengths of whose bases equals $k$. Prove that the extensions of the lateral sides of all such trapezoids pass through one point.

100 white points stand around a circle. Anya and Borya take turns painting one not yet painted point red or blue; Anya starts. Anya wants to end up with as many pairs of differently coloured neighbouring points as possible, and Borya wants as few such pairs as possible. What is the largest number of pairs of differently coloured neighbouring points that Anya can guarantee herself regardless of Borya's play?

All positive integers from 1 to 1000 are written in a row in some order, each exactly once. Prove that one can choose several consecutive numbers of the row whose sum is greater than 100000 but does not exceed 100500.

The diagonals of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ are perpendicular and meet at a point $O$. The incentres of the triangles $ABC$, $BCD$, $CDA$, $DAB$ are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral whose perimeter equals $P$. Prove that the sum of the inradii of the triangles $AOB$, $BOC$, $COD$, $DOA$ does not exceed $\frac{P}{2}$.

Sergey claims that he has found distinct real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that
$$\frac{1}{x^2 + x + 1} + \frac{1}{y^2 + y + 1} + \frac{1}{z^2 + z + 1} = 4.$$
Can Sergey's words be true?

Petya claims that he wrote 10 consecutive positive integers and it turned out that among all the digits used in these numbers each digit (from 0 to 9) occurs the same number of times. Could Petya's words be true?

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $\angle A = \angle C = 90^\circ$ is given. It is known that its vertices $A$ and $D$ together with the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $BC$ lie on one circle. Prove that the vertices $B$ and $C$ together with the midpoints of the sides $AD$ and $DC$ also lie on one circle.

Find all triples of (not necessarily distinct) positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ such that each of the numbers $a + bc$, $b + ca$, $c + ab$ is a prime divisor of the number $(a^2 + 1)(b^2 + 1)(c^2 + 1)$.

Each of 2024 people is a knight or a liar. Some of them are friends with each other, and friendship is mutual. Each of them was asked about the number of his friends, and all the answers were distinct integers from 0 to 2023. It is known that all knights answered the question correctly, and all liars changed the true answer by exactly 1. What is the smallest possible number of liars among these people?
A quadratic trinomial $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ has two distinct real roots $x_1$ and $x_2$. It is known that $f(x_1 + x_2) = 2025$. What can $c$ be equal to?

A country has 30 cities and 30 two-way air routes joining the cities in a cycle. Is it possible to add 10 more air routes so that afterwards one can get from any city to any other with at most 4 flights?
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $a^2b + b^2c + c^2a = 2$ and $ab^2 + bc^2 + ca^2 = 4$. Prove that some two of the numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ differ by more than 2.
Is it possible to mark finitely many nodes of the infinite square grid so that at least two points are marked and for any pair of marked points there is a marked point equidistant from them?

The altitudes $BD$ and $CE$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$, the altitudes of the triangle $ADE$ meet at a point $F$, and the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$. Prove that $BH + CH \geqslant 2FM$.

Initially the number 0 is shown on a display. When a button is pressed, the number on the display changes by 50 or by 51. The button was pressed 2025 times. Could the number 25 be shown on the display after this, if it is known that no numbers with more than two digits and no negative numbers ever appeared on the display?

A trapezoid $ABCD$ is given. It is known that $\angle DAB = \angle ABC = 90^\circ$, and the bisectors of the angles $C$ and $D$ meet at a point $E$ lying inside the trapezoid. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $ABE$ and $CDE$ touch each other.

Each cell of a $2 \times 100$ grid rectangle is painted white or black. A domino is a $1 \times 2$ or $2 \times 1$ grid rectangle. It turned out that there is a unique way to divide the given $2 \times 100$ rectangle into dominoes so that each domino covers at least one black cell. What is the largest possible number of black cells?

Call a positive integer one-sided if it is greater than 1 and all its prime divisors end in the same digit. (For example, the numbers 19 and $117 = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 13$ are one-sided, while the number $682 = 2 \cdot 11 \cdot 31$ is not.) Does there exist an increasing arithmetic progression with common difference not exceeding 2025 consisting of 150 positive integers each of which is one-sided?

1000 distinct points whose abscissae are integers from the segment $[0; 100000]$ are marked on the graph of the function $y = x^2$. Prove that one can choose six distinct marked points $A$, $B$, $C$, $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ such that the areas of the triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are equal.
Six consecutive positive integers are given. Prove that they can be labelled (in some order) $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$, $f$ so that the number $\frac{a}{b+c} + \frac{d}{e+f}$ is a positive integer.

Dasha and Sasha each have a $9 \times 9$ board. Dasha places 40 non-overlapping $1 \times 2$ tiles on her board (so that the tiles occupy 80 cells and one cell remains uncovered). Let her have $D$ ways to do this. Sasha paints 41 unit boundary segments between neighbouring cells on her board so that for every cell of the board at least one of its sides is painted. Let Sasha have $S$ ways to do this. Prove that $S \leqslant 2D$.

The perimeter of a convex pentagon $ABCDE$ equals 2. Let $O_a$, $O_b$, $O_c$, $O_d$, $O_e$ be the circumcentres of the triangles $EAB$, $ABC$, $BCD$, $CDE$, $DEA$, respectively. Let $M_a$, $M_b$, $M_c$, $M_d$, $M_e$ be the midpoints of the segments $AO_a$, $BO_b$, $CO_c$, $DO_d$, $EO_e$, respectively. Prove that
$$M_aM_b + M_bM_c + M_cM_d + M_dM_e + M_eM_a \geqslant 1.$$
Does there exist a positive integer $n$ such that for some three of its divisors $a$, $b$, $c$, greater than 1, the product $(a - 1)(b - 1)(c - 1)$ is divisible by $n^2$?

Middle-earth has 1000 counties, in one of which the magic Ring is located. Once a day the Wizard may choose any subset of the counties and receive from the magic Stone an answer as to whether the Ring is in one of these counties. The Stone may err, but it never errs two days in a row. The Wizard may perform this action for some number of days, after which he must send messengers to some $k$ counties, in one of which the Ring is certainly located. For what smallest $k$ can the Wizard do this?

16 points dividing a circle into 16 equal arcs are marked on it. Petya placed at these points (in some order) 16 consecutive positive integers. Then for each pair of diametrically opposite points Petya computed the sum of the numbers at these points. Could the 8 sums obtained be 8 consecutive positive integers?

A line $ax + by + c = 0$ is drawn in the coordinate plane, where $a$, $b$, $c$ are some positive numbers. It is known that this line touches the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. Prove that three segments with lengths $a$, $b$, $c$ can be put together to form a right triangle.

2026 mathematicians take part in a conference, each of whom has some number of friends (possibly none) among the others. Friendship is mutual. It is known that the following condition holds: if two mathematicians are friends, then their numbers of friends differ by exactly 1. Find the largest possible number of pairs of friends.

An acute scalene triangle $ABC$ with $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$ is given. The points $D$ and $E$ are symmetric to its circumcentre $O$ with respect to the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The line $DE$ meets the segments $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $F$ and $G$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $BDF$ and $CEG$ touch each other.

A polynomial $f$ of degree three with integer coefficients is given, whose leading coefficient equals 1 or $-1$. It is known that $f$ has three distinct roots, each of which is the square of a positive integer. Prove that the sequence of values $|f(1)|, |f(2)|, |f(3)|, \ldots$ contains the square of a positive integer.
